fields.title: About us
fields.hero.intro: A word from the president, and the values and mission of the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation.
content: A word from the president

Dear friends,
Dear friends,

The Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation is a non-governmental organisation working in Cameroon to nurture vocations, develop talent and share knowledge. It draws on the generous spirit of my father, Jean-Félicien Gacha, who lived by a phrase that is dear to me: we must help others, listen to others, respect others, heal others… and above all, love others.

We work in five main areas: education and training, culture and crafts, health and social action, environment and farming, and community tourism. In everything we do, we are committed to sharing knowledge, encouraging know-how and passing it on, so that people can grow. We will be delighted to welcome you to the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation, to discover and share all of our activities.
Welcome to our website!

Ly Dumas
President of the Foundation
Portrait of Ly Dumas, President of the NGO Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation.
Values, mission and objectives

The Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation stands 1,500 metres above sea level on the heights of the village of Bangoulap, near the town of Bangangté, in West Cameroon. This region is known as the “Grassland” because of its green and fertile land.

A non-profit organisation, it was created in 2002 to carry on the work of Jean-Félicien Gacha (1922–1972), senior civil servant, great builder, francophile and upright patriot. Throughout his life he showed a deep humanism, helping his fellow citizens to learn and to develop.
Portrait of Jean-Félicien Gacha.
Since 26 February 2014, the Foundation has held NGO status, granted by Cameroon’s Ministry of Territorial Administration and Decentralisation (MINATD).
View of the facilities of the NGO Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation, 2017.
The Foundation’s vision is to “nurture vocations and develop talent”.
Its work in Cameroon brings this vision to life. It is organised around three families of objectives: HEAD, HAND and HEART.
HEAD: sharing knowledge
– Promoting culture and traditional knowledge
HAND: encouraging know-how
– Encouraging education and training
– Teaching young people to be versatile
HEART: helping people grow
– Supporting social action for community development
– Working for living together through intercultural exchange
The Foundation employs committed people, recruited to bring its many activities to life.
The Foundation invests (buildings and equipment, passing on donated materials) and supports community projects (volunteer missions, work in the general interest, and more).

fields.title: Facilities
fields.hero.intro: The JLD Culture Centre, auditorium, library, collection, botanical garden and heritage huts: the Foundation’s spaces in Bangoulap.
content: The JLD Culture Centre

The JLD Culture Centre is the main building of the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation. It was built to pass on knowledge in many fields to younger generations, with high-quality facilities. A gift from the Arstarté gallery was essential to its completion.
The JLD Culture Centre offers training in its workshops. It is also a meeting place for young people who want to enjoy its facilities and programme, on their own or with their school.
View of the JLD Culture Centre and its workshops.
The auditorium
The heart of the JLD Culture Centre, the auditorium hosts lectures, debates, performances, concerts and film screenings.
The Harth library

The library was built in 2012 thanks to a gift from Mr and Mrs Harth. It offers everyone a large collection of books – general literature, children’s books, school books… – many of them given by donors.
The computer room
The computer room is open to everyone. Computer training is also offered.
The Ly and Frédéric Dumas Collection
An exhibition space showcases objects, costumes and traditional sculptures that bear witness to the richness and quality of craftsmanship, especially beadwork.
The multisports ground
Open to all members of the JLD Culture Centre, the sports ground overlooks the Foundation. It is the first step of a project to offer a complete sports facility.
The FOUDJEM children’s house

Opened in 2017, the main room of this building for young children was named “Salle Marcel et Ulo Zwingmann”, in tribute to the gift from the Zwingmann Foundation that made it possible. Its spaces and equipment are dedicated to children.
The botanical garden and the medicinal plants laboratory

A botanical garden and a laboratory with more than 420 plant varieties were created at the heart of the Foundation, for education – passing on knowledge –, for health – preparing therapeutic decoctions and herbal teas – and for conserving and protecting natural heritage.
The heritage huts

Examples of vernacular architecture have been rebuilt on the Foundation’s grounds to show past and present know-how that is disappearing. The traditional huts (Mousgoum, Bamiléké, Bororo) illustrate the architectural richness of Cameroon.

Buy the book Perles, Couleurs d’Afrique – €100

You can buy the book Perles, couleurs d’Afrique (Beads, Colours of Africa); all profits go to the Espace Culturel Gacha to fund its activities. It is sold by the association for €100, membership included.

It reveals the collections of beaded objects and the personal creations of its author, Ly Dumas. The book looks at the bead, its history, its symbolism and its central place in Africa in a poetic and aesthetic way.

Perles, couleurs d’Afrique is the first book devoted to Ly Dumas’s work and passion. This “art object” book tells the story of her passion for beads and reveals her collections and creations through photographs and texts by a specialist in the art of beadwork, Professor Jean-Paul Notué. It offers a deep and beautiful insight into the world of African craftsmanship.

Published by Gourcuff Gradenigo
Released in December 2009
Size: 27 × 29 cm, about 200 pages
Bilingual French / English
With contributions from: Jean-Paul Notué, PhD in art history, anthropology and museology, who introduces each of the book’s three parts with a scholarly and aesthetic commentary. Francine Vormèse, journalist, who paints an original portrait of Ly Dumas in a delightful, lively text. Brigitte Gacha, PhD in literature, poet, author of Le Masque du Hibou. Her text Le dit de la perle tells, as a poetic tale, the story of the bead through the ages and its symbols.
OUR PARTNERS

MINEFOP (Cameroon’s Ministry of Employment and Vocational Training): the JLD Culture Centre is approved by MINEFOP
for the vocational training it provides. AGIR abcd (an association of retired volunteers working for cooperation and development): retired volunteers share their experience across the Foundation’s fields of work.

The French Institute of Cameroon: part of the network of French cultural institutions under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in Africa and around the world. The partnership allows the Foundation to host writers in residence at Villa Boutanga.
La Route des Chefferies (museum, cultural and tourism programme): travellers can stop at the Foundation during its tours.
Université des Montagnes: an animal production unit has been made available to veterinary students. Many other projects are run with the university.
We have also worked with valued partners on one-off cultural events:

IAM Intense Art Magazine: Ly Dumas’s work is featured in the first issue dedicated to Cameroonian women; the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation took part in the exhibition held at the MAM gallery in Douala in October 2015.
Little Africa: as part of its off-site cultural programme, Espace Culturel Gacha offers its members guided tours of Little Africa to discover Africa in Paris.
Afro-Polis: the Foundation has taken part in successive editions of this festival, which presents African culture in all its forms (crafts, design, literature, food…).

The Musée du Quai Branly – Jacques Chirac, in Paris, when its audio guide was redesigned in 2011, with a commentary on the beaded statue of Queen Bansoa. Since 2017 the museum shop has also sold pieces from the Foundation’s craft workshops. The Foundation’s president is a member of the board of the Société des Amis du Musée du Quai Branly.

Podcast ‘Perles d’Afrique’ #1: Igénie Nomba, the art of beadwork
Length: 3 min 14
Produced by Bruno Reguet
> Listen and share on Spotify: https://spoti.fi/2LgPfu1
Transcript (translated from French):

“Let’s say it happened like a love story – I didn’t even know it was called a bead. I just saw beaded objects and loved them; I saw them in traditional settings. I liked them very much and often wanted to touch them, but people here often speak of mysticism around these objects, so we were afraid to touch them. So when I discovered this workshop in Bafoussam, I said to myself: well, ordinary people can work with beads. Since that day I have been working with beads, and I am growing old with them. In the past, to work with beads you had to be a craftsman of the King’s Court, for example; to make these traditional objects you had to live at the King’s Court. But now, whatever your social class, you can work with beads. I like religious music when I bead… gospel. We bead on everything: calabashes, canes, thrones, traditional fabrics, headdresses, sneakers, bracelets, traditional musical instruments too, and giant bracelets. Here we will work with white and blue beads, the colours of our traditional cloth, ndop, with the double-serpent motif generally used by the Bamoun people. Oh yes, it’s very meticulous work that takes a lot of patience, and really, if you’re not patient, as I said, you won’t manage. Now and then I think of breaking up this love story between the bead and me, but I can’t. I love it so much! And I believe it loves me too.”
Podcast ‘Perles d’Afrique’ #2: Gilbert Ouembe, the art of ironwork
Length: 3 min 09
Produced by Bruno Reguet
> Listen and share on Spotify: https://spoti.fi/2LgPfu1
Transcript (translated from French):

“I arrived in Bangoulap on 27 July 1998, still very young – even today I’m not very tall. I worked, made the plates, ran some errands. But little by little I kept feeling that there was something I had to develop. I always felt that I had to do something; I had the impression I was creating, but I didn’t yet know what – I had to create, I always felt inside that I must create. Madame Dumas had her great vision too; one day she said to me: Gilbert, you must do something, you must do something, you can do it. That is where the real encouragement came from, and from there came the idea of the figures, because I always loved drawing and always liked going to cultural places. Now I keep creating Bamiléké figures. I tried this figure and it works. I keep moving forward; today I can hardly keep count because I’ve made so many. There are paramount chiefs, notables, warriors, I mean, and their appearance is solemn, because when you see a figure like this one, the appearance is so solemn – no ceremony happens by chance. It’s true that when you see all these figures dressed in ndop, with the elephant mask, big special bracelets, belts, distinctions, it is not by chance. Paramount chiefs, sub-chiefs and great notables wear them, and only those who have earned them can wear them – they cannot be worn without being earned. Even if you are the richest, you will never wear that without having earned it. The Fo’o! The name I can give is “the king!”, Fo’o! There, Fo’o – in French you would say “His Majesty the King”, in the local language Fo’o; everything that is Fo’o, in the West, means “King”. When you see the bells everywhere under his mask, it symbolises his wealth – it means he is rich, a happy man, a happy king. He can gather bells all over, to be exceptional, exceptional.”
Podcast #3: Benjamin Campaoré and botany
Length: 2 min 19
Produced by Bruno Reguet
> Listen and share on Spotify: https://spoti.fi/2LgPfu1
Transcript (translated from French):

“We already have more than 400 species on the Foundation’s site, and we keep increasing the number by propagating them. These are plants with many virtues. My name is Benjamin Campaoré. I come from Burkina Faso and arrived in Cameroon five years ago. I came to develop projects on the healing properties of medicinal plants. My idea was to develop the herbal tea project with Lippia alba, also called ‘brisée’. Next comes hibiscus, called ‘bissap’. And so on – we will have quite a few herbal teas at the Foundation, which could help treat malaria, fatigue and many other things. The Foundation’s aim is to carry out this project so that people who don’t have enough means can treat themselves with natural plants they find around their homes – naturally – and also to pass on to others the knowledge I gained from my father. He is a herbalist; he learnt it from his own father. I am proud to share this knowledge at the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation, so that the knowledge of my grandfather and my father lives on and helps others live. And with this better life, as I say, it can keep moving forward forever, without end.”

fields.title: Maison Gacha
fields.hero.intro: Maison Gacha is dedicated to preserving and promoting the craftsmanship and hand skills of Africa and beyond.
content: Maison Gacha is dedicated to preserving and promoting the craftsmanship and hand skills of Africa and beyond. Its work covers both tangible and intangible heritage. Maison Gacha holds a private collection of African art. Open to the contemporary and respectful of tradition, it exhibits, publishes, creates and shares. Its mission is carried out through a cultural programme on site and beyond – exhibitions, talks, artist residencies and workshops. Maison Gacha has its roots in the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation, in Bangoulap, Cameroon.

Maison Gacha works with craftswomen and craftsmen from many backgrounds. It develops, supports and encourages research and contemporary creation. These makers work materials in all their forms: iron, wood, textile, beads, clay. Through its work, Maison Gacha embraces intercultural exchange and the sharing of knowledge.
Maison Gacha will open its doors in Paris in 2025!

fields.title: Education
fields.summary: The Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation gives teaching and material support to schools in the region, including distributing equipment generously given by its donors.
content: The Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation gives teaching and material support to schools in the region, including distributing equipment generously given by its donors.
School support
It takes several forms.

The “Education for all” programme, set up to give a second chance to young people from Maka – the village next to the Foundation – who had dropped out of school, lets the Foundation help them catch up. Literacy classes for adults are also offered.
As part of a partnership, students from the Université des Montagnes give extra tuition to pupils who need it, especially at exam time.
The schools of Maka and Manoré
Access to schooling in Cameroon is a real challenge, made harder by the fact that many children, especially in the Bororo community, have no birth certificate – which they need to sit exams.

Maka is one of the Foundation’s historic education sites. Donations from Réna and Jean-Louis Dumas were vital while its school was being built, and since it opened in 2005, hundreds of children have been taught there.
In 2012, Maka primary school was handed over to the State (Ministry of Basic Education). It nevertheless remains under the Foundation’s protection, which continues to support its staff.
In 2014, the Foundation funded a new primary school in Manoré, allowing more than a hundred more children to go to school without travelling to Maka.
By 2016, most children from Maka and Manoré had attended schools supported by the Foundation, and many of them completed primary school.
Thanks to the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation, Manoré has a primary school and a nursery school, with a head teacher who teaches all the classes.

In September 2018, Manoré’s nursery pupils started the school year in a brand-new building built for them. It was opened in the presence of families and the teams of the Jean-Félicien Gacha Foundation and Espace Culturel Gacha.
Other schools and nurseries in the region are not forgotten: the Foundation regularly helps them carry out their projects.

fields.title: Vocational training
fields.summary: All year round, the JLD Culture Centre runs short training courses that help young people gain professional, state-recognised skills, taught by volunteers from the French association AGIRabcd.
content: All year round, the JLD Culture Centre runs short training courses. They help young people gain professional skills and access qualifying training. The courses are taught by volunteers from the French association AGIRabcd.

The JLD Centre is a private training centre (CPF-JLD). In 2010 the Foundation was approved by Cameroon’s Ministry of Employment and Vocational Training (MINEFOP). Its practical courses are therefore recognised by the State in the following trades: garment making, farming and livestock, secretarial and office skills, basketry, masonry, plumbing, woodwork, metalwork and beadwork.

fields.summary: The Foundation raises awareness of sustainable farming and runs training in agriculture and livestock.
content: In the field of the environment, the Foundation raises awareness of sustainable farming and runs training in agriculture and livestock.
Developing crops and livestock
The Foundation keeps a herd of dairy cows, aiming for a degree of food self-sufficiency and possibly to sell its farm produce.

fields.title: Health & social action
fields.summary: Discussion groups for women, awareness debates and donations of medical equipment to the region’s hospitals and health centres.
content: Prevention and social action

The JLD Culture Centre organises discussion groups for women, similar to family planning sessions. Planned by the Foundation or at the request of local partners, awareness debates are also held on topics such as girls’ education, early marriage, child nutrition and cholera.
Equipment support

Thanks to its network of partners and donors, the Foundation has for many years distributed medical equipment to the hospitals of the division and to the Bangoulap integrated health centre. These donations are often handed over at the General Assemblies.

fields.title: Community tourism
fields.summary: Villa Boutanga, the Foundation’s 26-room guesthouse in the hills, welcomes visitors to discover West Cameroon and its artistic, culinary and natural traditions.
content: The Foundation runs a 26-room guesthouse: Villa Boutanga. Visitors enjoy a beautiful site in the heart of the hills, surrounded by nature, and discover West Cameroon and its artistic, culinary and landscape traditions… Since it opened, Villa Boutanga has welcomed thousands of visitors from around the world.

It has also allowed the Foundation to contribute to highlights of Cameroon’s cultural life: the Bangoulap Tour, a cultural hike promoting the sites of the Ndé region, and the Trail du Cameroun organised by the Club Sportif Automobile du Littoral…
